job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Nora Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a housing association in Leicester, in the finance team, tracking rent arrears and budget lines for about forty estates. I studied finance at a university in the Midlands, passed with an ordinary result and no internships, and have been here four months. I share a three-bed terrace with two friends, and my mum, a nurse on night shifts, texts me every morning. I run in the evenings and I help at a tenants' advice drop-in on Thursdays, which is the best part of my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, good, but let's not pretend nothing has changed already. I use a chatbot now and then to summarise long reports before a meeting. At work I'd say it's a useful tool, not magic, and my team would probably nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means very little for me yet. The arrears work is detailed and the tenants are people, not numbers. But I do notice that the boring first drafts of my reports take less time than in September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, mostly. I'd keep using the chatbot for summaries, check everything it gives me, and carry on saving about 300 a month toward a deposit. I'd also ask to sit in on more of the tenant meetings, because that's where I learn the most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a relief, because I like this job and I don't want it turned upside down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting AI aside, what about the next two years do you actually lose sleep over, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I do think about is housing costs. Rent in the city went up again, and my share is 480. Even with savings of around eleven thousand, I can't see how I'd ever buy a place near here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight or work got harder anyway, who or what would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, honestly. Decades of not building enough homes and letting landlords charge what they like. AI isn't why my generation is stuck.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool**, not magic, and I'd keep checking its work.
I'd tell colleagues it already saves me time on long reports.
think: The arrears work is **detailed** and about real tenants, so little changes for me.
I do notice my first drafts take **less time** than in September.
do: Keep using the chatbot for summaries and **check everything** it gives me.
Save **300 a month** toward a deposit and sit in on more tenant meetings.
feel: **Calm**, glad this job isn't turned upside down.
S0.quote: Decades of not building enough homes and letting landlords charge what they like. AI isn't why my generation is stuck.
fieldNote: **Steady** and practical: tries tools, verifies them, doesn't overclaim.
Her real pressure is **housing costs**, not AI.
Likes the people side of her job, which anchors her.

steps.text: Keep using the chatbot for report summaries and check the figures
Save 300 a month toward a deposit
Sit in on more tenant meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit some jobs hard and the people running it should have to plan for that. At work I'd bring it up at our staff forum. If the association starts using software to chase arrears, the tenants need a human to talk to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the number-crunching part of my job could be taken over in a few years. The budgets and the arrears reports are exactly what software is good at. What I'd have left is the people part, and that's smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more, deliberately, so I'm the person who knows how to check it. I'd ask to move toward tenant support and policy analysis. I'd also join the union branch, since the staff forum alone has no teeth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I keep running the numbers on which of us the finance team would still need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week would software take over first, and would anyone notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of the three junior roles are mostly report-building, and that's the first part software would take. Our manager might not replace the older colleague who retires next year. Nobody would announce it, we'd just notice an empty desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to do, if you could ask for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training time in work hours, paid for by the association, and an agreement that savings from software go partly into keeping people. If it only goes into profit, it's a bad deal.

say: I'd say employers should **plan** for the jobs hit and that tenants need a human.
I'd raise it at the staff forum and push for a union branch.
think: The **number-crunching** in my job could be taken over, leaving the smaller people side.
I keep working out which of us the team would still **need**.
do: Use AI more on purpose, so I'm the one who can **check** it.
Join the union branch and ask to move toward **tenant support**.
feel: **Uneasy** but not scared, with a nagging feeling about the team.
S1.quote: Two of the three junior roles are mostly report-building, and that's the first part software would take.
fieldNote: **Calm** about her own job but sees where the team shrinks.
Plans to be the checker of AI output and to move toward people work.
Joins collective action as a practical lever, not a cause.

steps.text: Learn to check AI-built reports against the raw arrears data
Ask to move toward tenant support work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government is nowhere near ready and that's the scandal. Two years, and we have no plan for jobs, no plan for income, nothing. I'd sign every petition for a public plan and share it with friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my finance degree might be nearly worthless by then. I've only just started and I'd be competing with something that does reports in seconds. It feels like I've been handed a ticket for a train that's already left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd put every spare penny into savings, which could stretch to about fourteen thousand. I'd ask my mum what the hospitals will want in two years, because care work seems safer. I'd also volunteer more at the advice drop-in, since helping people is useful in any world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Anxious and a bit angry that nobody asked us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do in the first month after you hear it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my housing association's director about what happens to our team. Then I'd look at nursing or social work as a plan B, but I wouldn't quit yet. I'd keep the job as long as it exists because the pay is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your family, and what do you leave out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm worried but that I have savings and a plan. I'd leave out how much I'm worried she will be bankrolling me. Her pay isn't big either.

say: I'd say the government has **no plan** for jobs or income after two years.
I'd sign every petition for a public plan and share it.
think: My finance degree might be nearly **worthless**, and I'd be competing with something that works in seconds.
I feel handed a ticket for a train that has **left**.
do: Pour spare money into **savings** toward fourteen thousand and keep the job.
Look into **nursing or social work** as a plan B.
feel: **Anxious** and angry that nobody asked young people.
S2.quote: I've only just started and I'd be competing with something that does reports in seconds. It feels like I've been handed a ticket for a train that's already left.
fieldNote: Anxious, not alarmed: **savings** and a caring-work plan B give some control.
Her mum's nursing career shapes her idea of a safe job.
Political anger comes with concrete **petition** actions.

steps.text: Save every spare penny toward fourteen thousand
Research nursing and social work courses
Sign and share petitions demanding a public jobs plan
Volunteer more hours at the Thursday advice drop-in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same problem with a bit more time, so the government has to use that time. Five years is just enough to build retraining and a safety net, if they bother. I'd push for it, including through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more hopeful. Five years is long enough to be moved off number work and into something with people in it. I'd be twenty-seven, and still young enough to start again if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd move into a tenant-support role if one opens, keep using AI so I'm good at checking it, and start a part-time course in housing policy. I'd stay in the share to save, and keep the deposit money for a rainy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's room to prepare, but the end point still scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I wouldn't panic-sell my life plans. I'd probably still plan to buy somewhere, but a small flat, and later than I'd hoped. In two years I'd have frozen all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money go during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big chunk stays in savings. Some goes on the course, a bit on my mum's heating bill. I wouldn't invest in anything risky, because I need to be able to get hold of it quickly.

say: I'd say five years is **just enough** to build retraining and a safety net.
I'd push for that through the union and the staff forum.
think: Five years is long enough to move off **number work** and toward people work.
At twenty-seven I'd be young enough to **start again**.
do: Move into **tenant support** if a role opens and start a part-time housing policy course.
Keep using AI and stay in the share to save.
feel: **Uneasy**: room to prepare, but the end point still scares me.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to be moved off number work and into something with people in it.
fieldNote: More **hopeful** than in the two-year world.
Extra time lets her keep a (smaller, later) home-buying plan alive.
Still cautious: no risky investing, savings kept **liquid**.

steps.text: Move into a tenant-support role when one opens
Start a part-time housing policy course
Keep the deposit money in an easy-access account
Use AI daily and keep checking its work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it well. I'd say retraining, a shorter week and fair taxes on firms that profit should be settled well before the end of it. And I'd say we shouldn't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. At thirty-two I'd probably be in policy or tenant services. The risk is that people assume there's time and do nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: finish the housing course, move into policy over three or four years, save for a small flat. I'd use AI openly and teach newer colleagues how to check it. And I'd keep helping at the drop-in, because it's why I like this work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. Not carefree, but I can see a way through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What can you do with that time that you couldn't with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I could do a master's in public policy part-time, and maybe get into the council or a charity. In two years that route would be closed, because there'd be no time to build up a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still want to be in this kind of work by then, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in finance reports, no. I'd want to be where decisions about housing get made. I think someone who understands both the numbers and the tenants will still be wanted.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if retraining and fair taxes are settled early.
I'd say we shouldn't wait for the final years.
think: I'd probably be fine, in **policy or tenant services** by thirty-two.
My real worry is that people assume there's time and do **nothing**.
do: Finish the housing course and move into **policy** over three or four years.
Teach newer colleagues how to **check** AI output and keep helping at the drop-in.
feel: Fairly **calm**; I can see a way through it.
S4.quote: I think someone who understands both the numbers and the tenants will still be wanted.
fieldNote: Time converts her worry into a **career plan**.
Wants to move from finance reports to housing policy.
Concerned that others will **drift** and do nothing, not so much about herself, which says a lot about her.

steps.text: Finish the housing course and apply for policy roles
Do a part-time master's in public policy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything piles into the same time frame: my degree, my job, my savings plan, and nobody has a plan. What would help is a public plan for income and retraining, plus a union that's actually at the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't want people my age to be written off. We're not lazy, we've just walked into a bad moment.

headlineQuote: We're not lazy, we've just walked into a bad moment.
portrait: Nora is 22, a junior finance officer at a Leicester housing association, four months into her first job.
She uses AI now and then, checks what it says, and treats it as a tool rather than magic.
Her politics lean left: she wants unions, regulation and a public plan, and blames government for the housing squeeze.
Eleven thousand in savings and plenty of local jobs keep her **calm** or uneasy in most worlds, anxious only at two years.
Her plan B is always people work, shaped by her nurse mother and her Thursday advice drop-in.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world worries her most, because degree, job and savings plan all collide in it.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **public plan** for income and retraining, and a union with a seat at the table.
